note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every count, address, rule and opening time below comes from the City of Kirkland's own pages: its pickleball page for the counts and the city-wide rules, and each park's own page for the address, the parking and the detail. Kirkland is a small city that documents its courts unusually well, and where it stays silent - on lighting, on cost, on surface - this page says so rather than filling the gap.

slots.parking: This is the best-documented parking of any city on this site, and it is documented because Kirkland chose to write it down rather than because anything here was worked out. Everest Park states it outright: "There are two parking lots at Everest with space for up to 100 vehicles." That is a real number for a real car park, and no other operator in this directory has published one. Peter Kirk Park is the opposite kind of answer and just as useful: it sits against downtown Kirkland, and the City directs you to "the Municipal Parking Garage or along Central Way" rather than to a lot of its own - a garage and a street, which is what parking at a downtown park actually means. Feriton Spur Park lists a parking lot among its amenities without sizing it. What none of the three pages states is whether any of it costs money or fills at a particular hour, and the Municipal Parking Garage is a City facility with its own rules that this page does not attempt to summarise. One further practical note the City does make: Peter Kirk Park is next door to the Kirkland Transit Center, so it is the one venue here reachable without a car on the City's own account.
slots.peak_hours: Every pickleball court in Kirkland closes at dusk. The City states it four times - once in the rules, once in each row of its table - and it is the single most important thing to know about timing here, because it means the courts have no evening session at all in winter and a long one in July. There is no opening variation to track: all three parks run 8 a.m. to dusk, every day. What the City publishes instead of crowd estimates is better than a guess, because it is the rule it enforces when courts fill. At Everest Park and on three of Peter Kirk's six courts, the posted rule is one game to 11 points and then rotate off if players are waiting. On the other three Peter Kirk courts, the rule is a 30-minute limit and then rotate. An operator does not write a rotation rule for courts that sit empty, and it does not split a six-court site into open-play and timed halves unless it expects a queue - so the honest reading is that Peter Kirk fills, and the City has planned for it rather than described it. What is genuinely absent is any statement of when. No Kirkland page names a busy morning, a league night or a weekend rush, and this page does not invent one.
slots.surface_condition: Kirkland states no surface for any of its courts, which is the ordinary case here. What it does state is age, and at two of the three venues that is the more useful fact. Peter Kirk Park's six courts are the newest in this entire directory: they were tennis courts until 13 April 2026, when the City closed them "for conversion to six dedicated pickleball courts", and they opened on 2 July 2026 at 3 p.m. Whatever surface they carry, it was laid this year. Feriton Spur Park's single court came out of a 2021-2022 renovation in which Google and SRM Development expanded the park, so it is recent too. Everest Park's three courts carry no date at all, though the City did replace that park's restroom in 2026. The one place Kirkland describes a playing surface rather than dating it is a court this site does not publish: Van Aalst Park has "half-basketball court with lines drawn for pickleball", which tells you exactly what you would be playing on and never says how many courts that amounts to.
slots.local_scene: Ten verified courts across three parks, which is a small inventory made interesting by how the City runs it. Kirkland's rule is that its pickleball courts are for drop-in play and nothing else: "All City of Kirkland pickleball courts are available on a first-come, first-served basis", and "The use of pickleball courts for business purposes is not allowed, including lessons, leagues, or tournaments." That is a firmer position than any other operator in this directory takes. Several cities here note that programming may limit public access; Kirkland has instead reserved every one of its courts for the public permanently and pushed the organised game elsewhere - it runs its own classes and leagues through kirklandparks.net, off these courts. The direction of travel is toward more pickleball rather than less. Six tennis courts at Peter Kirk Park became six dedicated pickleball courts this summer, a conversion the City documented step by step on the park's own page, and it is the only such conversion recorded anywhere on this site. Kirkland also has a claim on the sport's history that its own page makes: pickleball was invented in Washington, on Bainbridge Island in 1965, and became the official state sport in 2022. Kirkland is Washington's fourth city in this directory and the third in King County, after Seattle and Bellevue - both of which the City's own page points readers to under "Nearby Places to Play".

best_for.heading: Best if you want the newest courts in the city
best_for.text: Peter Kirk Park has six dedicated pickleball courts that opened on 2 July 2026, converted from the park's tennis courts that April. Three are open play and three are timed at 30 minutes when people are waiting. It is next to downtown, the transit centre and the library, with a year-round restroom and public Wi-Fi, and it is open 8 a.m. to dusk daily.

best_for.heading: Best if you are driving
best_for.text: Everest Park has three pickleball courts and, unusually, a stated car park: the City says there are two lots with space for up to 100 vehicles. Add year-round restrooms replaced in 2026, ballfields, a playground and a picnic shelter. All three courts are open play, drop-in only, 8 a.m. to dusk.

best_for.heading: Best for a quick hit, not a rotation
best_for.text: Feriton Spur Park has one court - the City describes it as "a 44-foot pickleball court", which is the regulation length of exactly one. The park was rebuilt by Google and SRM Development in 2021-2022 and carries a paved trail, an urban farm, a splash area, a zip-line and year-round bathrooms. One court means one game.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Kirkland have?
faqs.a: Ten across three City parks: six at Peter Kirk Park, three at Everest Park and one at Feriton Spur Park. The City lists exactly those three on its pickleball page. A fourth park, Van Aalst, has pickleball lines drawn on a half-basketball court, and because the City never says how many courts that is, it is not published here.

faqs.q: Which Kirkland park has the most courts?
faqs.a: Peter Kirk Park, with six, at 202 3rd St next to downtown. They are also the newest courts in this directory - the City converted its tennis courts there and reopened them as pickleball courts on 2 July 2026.

faqs.q: Is it free to play in Kirkland?
faqs.a: The City states no charge for any of its pickleball courts, but it also never says they are free, so this site does not describe them as free. Note that the "Free Play" schedule on Everest Park's page is about field time on grass and turf, not about the pickleball courts.

Not stated, and in practice it does not arise: every court is open only from 8 a.m. to dusk, so there is no session after dark to light. Peter Kirk Park does have a lighted baseball field, which is not the same thing and is not recorded as one.

No. All Kirkland pickleball courts are first-come, first-served and drop-in only. The City goes further and prohibits business use of the courts entirely, including lessons, leagues and tournaments - it runs its own classes and leagues separately through kirklandparks.net.

faqs.q: What happens if the courts are full?
faqs.a: The City posts a rotation rule. At Everest Park, and on the three Peter Kirk courts nearest the skate park, play one game to 11 points and then rotate off. On the three Peter Kirk courts nearest the street, play is limited to 30 minutes.
8 a.m. to dusk, every day, at all three parks. The City states it as a city-wide rule as well as in each row of its table.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring a net?
faqs.a: Not at the three published venues, which have pickleball courts. At Van Aalst Park, which is not published here, the City says players must bring their own nets.
